summary.text:
A workmanlike strategy from a treasury team that discloses its edges more plainly than most. Three specific figures stand out: £17.372m outstanding premium from prior LOBO and market-loan restructuring, named explicitly at Appendix A p.6; £12.000m of LOBOs with lender call options in 2026/27, both of them (from a £18.500m at 6.16% LOBO book) sat at rates well above market so 'unlikely to be recalled' per Appendix B p.20; and £24.000m of the £365.606m Authorised Limit is explicitly earmarked for the DSG deficit at Appendix A p.7 — most authorities do not itemise DSG headroom that way, they fold it into general liquidity.

The DSG deficit itself sits at £20.000m at 31.03.26 and 'increasing by approximately another £8.000 million during 2026/27' (App A p.6). It is outside the CFR (which never captures revenue deficits) but drives external borrowing to maintain liquidity. The paper does not name a DSG statutory override end date — only the CCLA pooled-fund override is dated (extended to 31 March 2029, para 1.18 of covering).

Balance-sheet identity ties exactly across all five years — CFR less loans less PFI reproduces the internal-borrowing line to within £1k in each. Liability-benchmark identity ties equally cleanly (Loans CFR less balance-sheet resources plus £15m liquidity = £212.337m / £214.569m / £245.492m / £249.967m / £248.875m across 24/25 to 28/29). The workings are clean.

PWLB loan-book reconciliation FAILS. Their Appendix B Table 3 prints PWLB £150.020m at 3.99% at 31.12.25; our file at the same date holds 13 loans totalling £68.145m at 4.05%, and at 31.03.26 holds 26 loans totalling £168.583m at 4.06%. Same shape as the Leicester failure — our file appears to be anchored to drawdown-start dates that miss the pre-existing long-dated PWLB tail. Recorded in the note; kept out of the email; coverage gap disclosed once in the draft without soliciting correction. Break costs (indicative £3.780m net discount across 24 live loans, 10 below par 14 above) held internally for the same reason.

Rate view: the paper leans on the Arlingclose January 2026 forecast (App B p.13) of two more Bank Rate cuts to 3.25% by June 2026, held at 3.25% for three years. Six months on, Bank Rate has been 3.75% since the December 2025 cut; June 2026 came and went without a cut. That is a dated, testable position the paper takes, and the answer is in.

Distinctive smaller items: (i) the interest-rate exposure indicator is asymmetric — £0.909m limit on a 1% rise, £0 on a 1% fall, explicitly framed on the net-borrower position (App B p.24); (ii) the financing-costs-to-net-revenue ratio falls from 14% to 12% between 25/26 and 26/27, but the paper is honest that this is Fair Funding inflating the denominator, not a real cost fall (para 1.14 covering); (iii) CFR peaks at £320.570m in 27/28 and then turns down, unusual within a strategy period; (iv) Redcar becomes the lead authority for Tees Valley Energy Recovery Ltd in 2026, seven North-East councils' partnership for waste energy — worth watching in future papers.

officer.subject: £12m of LOBOs with lender calls in 2026/27, and the shape behind them
officer.body:
Dear Phil,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Capital and Treasury Strategy that went to Governance Committee on 9 February and on to Council on 26 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is unusually candid — the outstanding restructuring premium is named explicitly, and the DSG deficit is broken out cleanly inside the Authorised Limit rather than folded into a general liquidity buffer — so this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

What drew our attention first is the £18.500m of LOBOs at a weighted 6.16% in Table 3 of Appendix B, and specifically the pair totalling £12.000m with a lender call in 2026/27. The paper's own view is that these are 'unlikely to be recalled' because the rates are above the market. That matches what we've seen. Of the councils we have read this year, twelve LOBO calls have landed in the same window and every one has been declined by the lender — Dexia's calls at Kent and Tameside, three rejected calls at Wolverhampton, one at Staffordshire, and KBC's two loans at Bath & NE Somerset went floating with six-monthly resets rather than a rate rise, among others. The pattern points the same way as your paper does. Worth watching for the call dates when they land.

Related, and only visible because Appendix A names it: the £17.372m net premium outstanding at 31 March 2026 from prior LOBO and market-loan restructuring. Naming a running premium balance separately from the CFR is unusual in the papers we've read — most councils either fold it into the general debt narrative or leave it inside the effective-interest line. Similarly, itemising the £24.000m DSG deficit as a distinct component of the £365.606m Authorised Limit at Appendix A p.7 — rather than absorbing it into a general liquidity buffer — is transparency that a member reading the indicators can actually use. Redcar's £20m-going-to-£28m DSG position and the way you disclose its liquidity impact reads as one of the clearer treatments of that pressure in the papers we're reading through this strategy season.

One piece of market context. Appendix B leans on the Arlingclose January 2026 forecast at Table 1: Bank Rate to 3.25% by June 2026 in the central case, held at 3.25% for three years. Six months on, Bank Rate is still 3.75% — no cut since December 2025, and June came and went without one. The forecast note itself flagged 'near-term upside risks have increased', so the direction is not surprising, but it does mean the balance-sheet framing at Appendix A Table 6 — the liability benchmark rising from £214.569m at 31.03.26 to £248.875m by 28/29 — will be sensitive to the pace at which the next refinancing tranche is drawn. The full curve and SONIA path are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

Where you might find us most useful is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, which prices every published council's PWLB book against the DMO's premature-repayment curve daily. One caveat we owe you before you look: our PWLB file for Redcar and Cleveland appears to be missing the historic long-dated tail that sits behind the £150.020m figure in your Table 3, so we're flagging that rather than presenting our figures as your position. Break costs there are indicative only and only the DMO can quote. What we can quote against the market with confidence is anything drawn during this strategy period, and the monthly sector totals at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — so a next-draw decision can be benchmarked against what the sector actually did that month.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway is becoming central to how the whole strategy is framed. An interactive version tied to our rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — for a council whose benchmark rises £34m in three years while its existing loan book runs off £63m, being able to move the reserves path and see the crossover shift is the useful thing.

On training, three look most relevant to Redcar. LOBO mechanics: call decisions in practice covers what to expect if either of the 2026/27 calls lands. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice sits directly on Appendix B Table 6 and the chart on p.17. Capital & Treasury Strategy — for members is written for the Governance Committee seat that scrutinises this paper. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: Capital and Treasury Strategy 2026/27 — Governance Committee, 9 February 2026, items 8.0 (covering) and 8.1 (Appendices A–D). At https://RCBC.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s10389/8-0-governance-committee-report-capital-and-treasury-strateg.pdf and https://RCBC.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s10390/8-1-capital-and-treasury-strategy-26-27.pdf.

officer.voice: Russell Tew, first-person. Not templated: no bold headers, no bulleted summary, contractions throughout. Leads with the LOBO call window and the cross-council pattern (something no single council can see), then the transparent premium/DSG disclosures as complements rather than criticisms, then the Arlingclose forecast as a testable data point, then the coverage-gap disclosure without inviting correction.
